analysis.one_liner: Caps what candidates pay for pre-election TV and radio ads at the station's lowest rate and blocks preemption.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee after one subcommittee hearing, with no cosponsors and no floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the rules for how much candidates pay to run ads on TV and radio in the weeks before an election. It would require stations to sell them time at the lowest rate the station charges anyone in that period, instead of peak election-season rates, and would bar stations from bumping a candidate's purchased airtime. It was never voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates for public office, especially challengers and underfunded campaigns, who could buy pre-election ad time at the station's cheapest rate rather than inflated election-season rates, and who could count on their purchased airtime actually airing. Voters would indirectly gain if political advertising became cheaper, easing the fundraising pressure on campaigns.

how_it_helps.text: Limits the cost to qualified candidates of broadcasting time for pre-election political advertising to the lowest rate charged for any time in the same period.
Prohibits any broadcast licensee from preempting — knocking off the air — time that a qualified candidate has purchased for campaign advertising.
Removes the 'class' limitation in the law's rate provision, so the lowest-rate guarantee applies across the station's rates rather than being confined within a class of time.

analysis.who_pays: Broadcast station owners, who would have to sell candidate ads at their lowest rate during the lucrative weeks before elections and could no longer preempt those ads to run higher-priced commercial advertising.

drawbacks.text: Stations would give up peak-rate revenue during election season and lose flexibility over their schedules, costs broadcasters have long argued reduce resources for news and programming — an objection an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
The bill lowers the price of political ads but does nothing to cap total campaign spending, so campaigns would still need large sums to compete on television.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a modest, targeted fix: it would make pre-election airtime affordable for candidates with small budgets and guarantee the ads actually run. The cost falls on a concentrated industry (station owners), and the public benefit is indirect — cheaper campaign speech rather than a direct benefit to households. It does not address the larger money-in-politics problem of total campaign costs.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing in August 1989, and never moved to the floor before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on April 11, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
On August 2, 1989, the Communications Subcommittee held hearings on the bill (printed as S.Hrg. 101-227).
The full committee never reported the bill, and neither the Senate nor the House ever voted on it before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadcast station owners, who kept charging peak election-season rates for candidate ads and kept the power to preempt candidate airtime, while campaigns continued to bear the higher cost of political advertising.

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee on his sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Referred it to the Communications Subcommittee, which held one hearing, but never reported the bill to the full Senate.

against.name: National Association of Broadcasters
against.what_they_did: Broadcasters have long opposed measures that cut the rates they can charge candidates or limit their control over airtime; no supporting activity for this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor with no cosponsors and no votes, so the record shows no party-line pattern either way.

industries.note: The bill would have cut what stations can charge candidates for pre-election ads to their lowest rate and barred them from preempting candidate airtime, reducing station revenue during the most lucrative advertising period. Their interest in keeping peak rates and preemption power runs against cheaper, more accessible campaign advertising for candidates and voters.

industries.industry: Political advertising and campaign media buyers
industries.note: Cheaper guaranteed airtime would lower campaign ad costs and could shift some spending decisions, but campaigns would still buy large volumes of ads either way.
